This is open, and cannot be resolved with a finite computation.
Let $x_1,\ldots,x_n\in \mathbb{R}^2$ and let $R(x_i)=\#\{ \lvert x_j-x_i\rvert : j\neq i\}$, where the points are ordered such that\[R(x_1)\leq \cdots \leq R(x_n).\]Let $g(n)$ be the maximum number of distinct values the $R(x_i)$ can take. Is it true that $g(n) \geq (1-o(1))n$?
#653: [Er97e]
geometry | 
distances
Erdős and Fishburn proved $g(n)>\frac{3}{8}n$ and Csizmadia proved $g(n)>\frac{7}{10}n$. Both groups proved $g(n) < n-cn^{2/3}$ for some constant $c>0$.

A partial proof 
claimed by Rafik Zeraoulia (using OpenAI GPT-5.6 Thinking).
 Summary:
 The paper gives a new partial result toward Erdős Problem #653 on planar distance-count spectra. The previously known estimate gives a defect of order $n^{2/3}$. The main result improves this exponent: for every $\varepsilon>0$, the defect can be taken of order $n^{\vartheta-\varepsilon}$, where
$\vartheta=\frac{6e-1}{8e-3}=0.8166799862\ldots.$
The proof starts from the pinned-distance counts $R_P(p)$ of an $n$-point planar set $P$. Assuming that too many pinned-distance values are missing below a threshold $T$, one selects more than $T/2$ centers whose pinned-distance counts realize distinct values. Around each selected center one considers the circles determined by the distances from that center to the remaining points.
This produces a point-circle incidence configuration with $M\ll T$ centers, at most $L\ll T^2$ circles, and at least $\gg Tn$ incidences. The key step is then to apply the Pach-Tardos restricted-center point-circle incidence bound while retaining the depe
 Notes:
 This submission should be regarded as a partial result rather than a complete solution of the problem. Its main contribution is the improved exponent $0.8166799862\ldots$, obtained by exploiting the restricted-center form of the point-circle incidence theorem more efficiently than in the standard argument. The supplementary structural lemmas are included because they may be useful for pushing the exponent further.
